newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Egypt presidents aim to break Mideast ice.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Egypt presidents aim to break Mideast ice.

text.p: President Ezer Weizman said on Thursday he hoped to help break the ice in Israeli peacemaking with the PLO by meeting Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak soon.

The planned meeting drew swift criticism from political sources close to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who sparked a crisis with the Arab world when he broke ground on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem two months ago.

"Through the meeting Egypt wants to use the president (Weizman) to assert the negative role it plays in the diplomatic process," one source said, accusing Egypt of trying to torpedo Israeli government efforts.
Weizman, an architect of Israel's landmark peace treaty with Egypt while a cabinet minister in 1979, told reporters Mubarak proposed in a phone call on Wednesday that they meet in Egypt.
In Cairo, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa confirmed the two presidents had spoken but said no meeting had been set for the next few days.
An aide to Weizman said he expected a meeting soon.

"I view this as another attempt to break some ice...It's important to all of us that the whole political process begin to move again. Will it move by way of President Mubarak or not? I don't know," the sharp-tongued Weizman said.

Weizman's job is largely ceremonial, so his contacts with Arab leaders, including meetings with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, underscore the crisis Netanyahu's 11-month-old right-wing government faces in peacemaking.

Asked if it were healthy for Weizman to meet Middle East leaders when Netanyahu was not, Weizman's director-general, Aryeh Shumer, told Israel Radio: "What do you want me to say -- that we are to blame for this?"

Weizman said he doubted Mubarak -- whom he described as a friend since the start of Israeli-Egyptian relations 20 years ago -- wanted to somehow portray the prime minister as less interested than Weizman was in pursuing peace.
"If anyone thinks that I am in the way, I want to hear it. I haven't heard it," Weizman said.
Netanyahu spoke with Mubarak by telephone later on Thursday but his office declined to disclose the content of the call.
Differences over Netanyahu's Jewish settlements policy have stalled negotiations with the PLO. Arafat met Mubarak in Egypt on Wednesday to discuss ways of reviving moribund talks.

Asked upon his return to Gaza about the prospects of convening an Arab summit to give some momentum to the peace process, Arafat said: "It is one of the things we discussed with all the options open."
An Israeli newspaper last week quoted Weizman as saying he had severed contacts with Netanyahu over the peace crisis.
The newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, quoted Weizman as having assailed Netanyahu, using his nickname "Bibi", by saying: "Bibi isn't ready to listen. He knows everything."

Weizman met Arafat earlier this month to try to break the impasse and the newspaper quoted him as saying: "When I returned from the meeting with Arafat, I thought he (Netanyahu) would want to hear what happened there. Not at all."
Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel told Reuters on Thursday that Netanyahu's office had been informed of the planned Mubarak-Weizman meeting.

Peacemaking ground to a halt when Netanyahu ordered work to begin on a new Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem on March 18. Netanyahu has said he is proud of the decision to build the 6,500-unit settlement.

Israel occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and claimed the whole city as its capital. The claim is not recognised internationally. Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state. They say settlement-building pre-empts final peace talks.
